draft.title: Symbols in film and images
card: A symbol in an image is an object, colour or setting that stands for an idea. Photos, paintings and films all use them.
A filmmaker can show an idea without a word. A stopped clock in a empty room might suggest that time has run out, or that someone is stuck in the past.
Close-ups, lighting and repetition draw the viewer's eye to a symbol. A closing door shown twice is likely to be more than a door.
To read a symbol, name what is shown, say the idea it suggests, then check that the rest of the image supports that idea.
draft.remember: An image can add meaning through objects, colours and settings that stand for ideas.

a.q: A film shows a girl leaving her home town. A close-up lingers on a door swinging shut behind her. What is the door most likely to symbolise?
opts: An ending, as she leaves her old life behind
A beginning, as she looks forward to a new home
Her wish to buy a new house in the city
Her fear of being locked inside a building
a.why: The close-up draws attention to the door, and it closes as she leaves. This suggests an ending to her old life. The second option is tempting, but nothing in the scene shows her looking ahead.
a.clue: Think about what is being left behind when the door shuts.

b.q: A photograph shows a lone boy on a bare, grey beach. A bright red kite lies on the sand beside him, its string snapped. What is the broken kite most likely to symbolise?
opts: A lost freedom or hope
A love of outdoor games
A warning about bad weather
The strength of the boy's family
b.why: The kite is bright against the grey beach, so it draws the eye. Its snapped string suggests that something free has been cut loose, so lost freedom or hope fits. A love of games does not fit, because the kite is broken and the boy is alone.
b.clue: Look at what has happened to the string, and at the colours around it.

a.best: An ending, as she leaves her old life behind

problems.detail: Grammar error: "a stopped clock in a empty room" should read "an empty room".

Why (a) calls the distractor "the second option", but the options are shuffled. Here the second option is the right answer, so the explanation would confuse students. It should name the distractor (the 'beginning' option) instead.
